title: Plants as Chemical Factories
summary: Why organisms make bioactive chemicals and how medicinal plant material is identified, harvested and authenticated.

lessons.title: Chemical Ecology: Why Plants Make Defensive Compounds

levels.kid:
Plants can't run away. When a hungry bug or deer comes along, a plant is stuck right where it is. So plants fight back with chemistry!

Plants make special chemicals that taste bad, make animals sick, or confuse them. A chili pepper's hot burn stops mice and many other animals from eating it. Birds don't feel the burn, though. They eat the peppers and spread the seeds far away.

Some plants even call for help. When caterpillars chew corn, the corn gives off a smell that brings tiny wasps to attack the caterpillars.

Some bugs fight back too. Monarch caterpillars eat a poisonous plant called milkweed and keep the poison inside them for protection.

Doctors use some of these plant chemicals as medicines, because they work on our bodies too.
levels.hs:
Plants are rooted in place, so they can't flee from insects, grazing animals or fungi. Many defend themselves with chemistry instead. Besides the **primary metabolites** every cell needs to grow (sugars, amino acids, fats), plants make **specialized metabolites** (older name: secondary metabolites). More than 200,000 are known, including alkaloids, terpenes and phenolics. Their main jobs are ecological: repelling attackers, attracting pollinators and shielding tissue from UV light.

Defenses come in two styles:
- **Constitutive** defenses are present all the time, like the tannins in oak leaves.
- **Induced** defenses switch on after damage. Chewing triggers the plant hormone **jasmonic acid**, which turns on defense genes.

Example: when a caterpillar chews a wild tobacco plant, the plant ramps up **nicotine**. Nicotine overstimulates the acetylcholine receptors in the insect's nervous system.

In 1964, Paul Ehrlich and Peter Raven proposed **coevolution**. Plants evolve new toxins, herbivores evolve resistance, and the cycle repeats like an arms race. Monarch butterflies are a famous winner: their caterpillars eat toxic milkweed and store its poisons for their own protection.

This matters for medicine. Plant toxins often hit proteins that are very similar in insects and people, such as receptors and ion channels. That is why so many plant chemicals, from morphine to atropine, became drugs.
levels.college:
**Chemical ecology** studies how chemicals mediate interactions between organisms. For plants the core logic is simple: being sessile, they invest in chemistry rather than escape.

**Avoiding self-poisoning.** A plant must store toxins without harming itself. Common solutions:
- **Two-component systems**: an inactive glycoside is stored apart from the enzyme that activates it. In the cabbage family, **glucosinolates** and the enzyme **myrosinase** sit in different cells; chewing mixes them, releasing pungent isothiocyanates (the "mustard oil bomb"). **Cyanogenic glycosides** in cassava and bitter almonds are hydrolyzed by beta-glucosidases to release **hydrogen cyanide**.
- Storage in vacuoles, resin ducts or glands, and attaching sugars (glycosylation) to lower toxicity.

**Induced signaling.** Wounded tomato leaves produce **systemin**, an 18-amino-acid peptide that activates jasmonate synthesis and systemic production of **proteinase inhibitors**, which block insect digestion. Jasmonates are the master regulators of defense against chewing insects; **salicylic acid** mainly coordinates defense against biotrophic pathogens.

**Indirect defense.** Turlings and colleagues (1990) showed that maize chewed by beet armyworm caterpillars releases volatiles that attract the parasitic wasp *Cotesia marginiventris*, a **tritrophic** interaction (plant, herbivore, predator).

**Directed deterrence.** Capsaicin activates the mammalian heat/pain receptor **TRPV1**, deterring seed-crushing rodents. Bird TRPV1 is insensitive, so birds swallow chilies and disperse the seeds intact.

**Counter-adaptation.** Milkweed cardenolides inhibit the **Na+/K+-ATPase** (sodium pump). Monarchs carry amino acid substitutions in this pump that block cardenolide binding, letting them sequester the toxins.

**Allocation.** Defense costs carbon and nitrogen. The **resource availability hypothesis** predicts that slow-growing plants in poor environments, where lost leaves are costly to replace, invest heavily in durable defenses. Fast growers in rich environments tend to tolerate damage and regrow.
levels.phd:
Gottfried Fraenkel's 1959 essay "The raison d'etre of secondary plant substances" reframed these compounds, long dismissed as metabolic waste, as defenses that shape insect host choice. Ehrlich and Raven (1964) extended this into escape-and-radiate coevolution, though phylogenetic tests show plant-herbivore diversification is often asymmetric or diffuse rather than strictly pairwise.

**Allocation theories** compete and overlap:
- **Apparency theory** (Feeny; Rhoades and Cates, 1976): long-lived, easily found plants use quantitative, dose-dependent defenses such as tannins; ephemeral plants use cheap qualitative toxins such as alkaloids or glucosinolates.
- **Optimal defense theory** (McKey 1974; Rhoades 1979): defenses concentrate in tissues with the highest fitness value and risk of attack, such as young leaves and flowers.
- **Resource availability** (Coley, Bryant and Chapin 1985) and **growth-differentiation balance** (Herms and Mattson 1992) link investment to growth rate and resource limitation.
None predicts well across all systems; costs are hard to measure, and ecological costs (lost pollinators, autotoxicity) may exceed metabolic ones.

**Jasmonate signaling.** Wounding and herbivore oral secretions trigger oxylipin synthesis from linolenic acid. The active hormone, **jasmonoyl-isoleucine (JA-Ile)**, acts as molecular glue between the F-box protein **COI1** (part of an SCF ubiquitin ligase) and **JAZ repressors**, which are then degraded by the 26S proteasome, freeing transcription factors such as **MYC2** to activate defense genes. JA and SA pathways are often mutually antagonistic, a trade-off attackers can exploit. Green and Ryan (1972) discovered wound-induced proteinase inhibitors in tomato; Pearce et al. (1991) identified systemin.

**Field validation.** Baldwin's group silenced putrescine N-methyltransferase in *Nicotiana attenuata*; nicotine-deficient plants suffered more herbivory in nature (Steppuhn et al. 2004), confirming function in situ.

**Target-site insensitivity.** Cardenolide resistance in the Na+/K+-ATPase alpha-subunit evolved convergently across insect orders, repeatedly at the same few positions (111, 119, 122). Karageorgi et al. (2019) engineered the monarch substitutions into *Drosophila*, producing resistant flies and revealing epistatic constraints on mutation order.

**Controversy.** Why so many compounds? The **screening hypothesis** (Jones and Firn 1991) argues few metabolites are potently active, and plants cheaply maintain chemical diversity that occasionally yields useful molecules; others argue most simply have undiscovered roles.
levels.expert:
For drug discovery, chemical ecology offers a practical heuristic: compounds selected to disrupt animals tend to hit evolutionarily conserved targets. Nicotine (nicotinic acetylcholine receptors), pyrethrins from *Tanacetum cinerariifolium* (voltage-gated sodium channels), caffeine (adenosine receptors, phosphodiesterases) and cardiac glycosides (Na+/K+-ATPase) act on proteins shared across phyla, which is why insect defenses become human drugs and poisons.

**Self-resistance as a target clue.** Producers must survive their own products. *Camptotheca acuminata* carries topoisomerase I substitutions that resist camptothecin, mirroring mutations in camptothecin-resistant tumor cells (Sirikantaramas et al. 2008). Searching producer genomes for resistant variants of conserved proteins is now used to infer the targets of uncharacterized natural products.

**Herbivores co-opt chemistry.** *Manduca sexta* larvae tolerate nicotine; a midgut cytochrome P450 (CYP6B46) helps shuttle ingested nicotine into hemolymph, and larvae exhale it to deter wolf spiders (Kumar et al. 2014). Defense compounds cascade through food webs.

**Not every compound is purely defensive.** Low nectar caffeine enhances honeybee memory of floral scent (Wright et al. 2013), so one molecule can repel herbivores and manipulate pollinators depending on concentration and tissue.

**Production and elicitation.** Because many pathways are inducible, methyl jasmonate is used to elicit secondary metabolism in plant cell cultures; it raises taxane yields in *Taxus* cultures, and paclitaxel is produced commercially by plant cell fermentation. Some pathway genes cluster physically in plant genomes (e.g., the noscapine cluster in opium poppy), aiding pathway discovery and transfer into yeast.

**Clinical relevance.** Insufficiently processed bitter cassava, rich in cyanogenic glycosides, is linked to **konzo**, an abrupt, irreversible spastic paraparesis in nutritionally stressed populations, particularly when the dietary sulfur amino acids needed to detoxify cyanide to thiocyanate are scarce.

**Pitfalls and open questions.** Induction means one species varies chemically with its damage history, complicating reproducibility of extracts. Lab bioactivity does not prove ecological function; knockouts tested in the field remain the gold standard. How plants generate chemical novelty (enzyme promiscuity, gene duplication) and whether ecological insight truly improves hit rates over random screening are still debated.

keyPoints: Plants are sessile, so many defend themselves with specialized (secondary) metabolites
Defenses are constitutive (always present) or induced after damage via jasmonate signaling
Two-component systems like glucosinolate-myrosinase avoid self-poisoning
Indirect defenses use volatiles to recruit predators and parasitoids of herbivores
Coevolution drives counter-adaptations such as monarch sodium-pump resistance to cardenolides
Plant toxins hit conserved animal targets, which is why many become medicines

test.q: Specialized (secondary) metabolites differ from primary metabolites because they:
choices: Are found mainly in animals rather than plants
Store energy as starch inside chloroplasts
Are required for basic growth and metabolism
Mediate defense and other ecological roles
test.explain: Specialized metabolites serve ecological jobs like defense, pollinator attraction and UV protection. Basic growth depends on primary metabolites.

Jasmonic acid
Salicylic acid
Gibberellic acid

Induced

choices: Separating a glucoside from its enzyme
Venting cyanide gas through leaf pores
Releasing sticky resin to trap the insects

test.explain: Glucosinolates and myrosinase are kept in different cells. Chewing mixes them and releases pungent isothiocyanates.

choices: They break down cardenolides in their gut
Milkweed stops making toxin when eaten
Their sodium pump has resistant mutations
They avoid the leaves containing toxin
test.explain: Cardenolides inhibit the Na+/K+-ATPase. Monarchs carry substitutions in this pump that block binding, so they can store the toxins rather than destroy them.

test.q: When caterpillars chew maize seedlings, the plants release volatiles that:
choices: Poison the caterpillars through the air they breathe
Make the leaves taste sweeter to the caterpillars
Warn the caterpillars to move to another plant

test.q: Capsaicin deters mammals but not birds. Why does this help the chili plant?
choices: Birds eat the insects that attack chilies
Mammals spread the seeds farther than birds
Birds disperse seeds without crushing them
Birds digest the seeds and add nutrients
test.explain: Bird TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin, so birds swallow chilies and spread intact seeds, while seed-crushing rodents are deterred.

test.q: Why do plant toxins so often work as human medicines?
choices: They are harmless to animal nervous systems
They target proteins conserved across animals
They were designed by plants to treat disease
They contain vitamins that humans lack
test.explain: Toxins evolved to disrupt herbivores hit receptors, channels and pumps shared by insects and humans. Plants did not evolve them to treat human disease.

test.q: According to the resource availability hypothesis, slow-growing plants in poor soils tend to:
choices: Lose leaves rapidly to save on defense
Invest less in defense than fast growers
Rely mainly on induced volatile signals
Invest heavily in long-lasting defenses
test.explain: Where lost leaves are costly to replace, plants protect them with durable defenses. Fast growers tend to tolerate damage and regrow.

test.q: Wounded tomato leaves produce ___, an 18-amino-acid peptide that triggers proteinase inhibitor production.
test.explain: Systemin activates jasmonate synthesis and systemic proteinase inhibitors that block insect digestion.

test.q: Ehrlich and Raven's 1964 study of butterflies and host plants proposed what idea of reciprocal evolutionary change between plants and herbivores?
test.explain: Coevolution describes plants evolving toxins and herbivores evolving resistance in repeated rounds.

test.q: Cassava and bitter almonds store cyanogenic glycosides that release hydrogen ___ when the tissue is crushed.
test.explain: Beta-glucosidases hydrolyze the glycosides, ultimately releasing hydrogen cyanide.

advancedTest.q: Camptotheca acuminata carries topoisomerase I mutations resembling those in camptothecin-resistant tumors. What does this best illustrate for drug discovery?

Plants evolve toxins to hit enzymes they do not themselves possess
Resistance mutations arise mainly after clinical use in patients

advancedTest.explain: A producer must protect its own copy of the target, so resistant variants in its genome point to what the compound hits. Topoisomerase I is conserved, not plant-specific.

choices: Old leaves about to fall
Young leaves and flowers
Woody stems near the soil
Mature leaves in deep shade
advancedTest.explain: Optimal defense theory places defenses where fitness value and attack risk are highest, such as young leaves and reproductive organs.

advancedTest.q: An Arabidopsis mutant lacking functional COI1 would most likely show:
choices: Increased MYC2 activity in undamaged leaves
Failure to degrade JAZ repressors after wounding
Constant high expression of jasmonate-responsive genes
Faster glucosinolate hydrolysis in intact cells
advancedTest.explain: COI1 is the F-box protein that, with JA-Ile, targets JAZ repressors for proteasomal degradation. Without it JAZ persists, MYC2 stays repressed and defense genes are not induced.

advancedTest.q: Manduca sexta larvae tolerate nicotine and exhale it to deter wolf spiders. Which conclusion best follows?
choices: Nicotine has little effect on insects and mainly targets mammals
Specialist herbivores can co-opt host toxins for their own defense
Induced defenses are useless once a specialist herbivore evolves
Wolf spiders are the main selective force shaping nicotine levels
advancedTest.explain: The larva turns the plant's toxin into its own anti-predator weapon, showing defense chemistry cascades through food webs. Field data show nicotine still reduces herbivory, so it is not useless.

lessons.title: Plant Anatomy for Drug Hunters: Trichomes, Latex, Bark and Roots

levels.kid:
Plants can't run away from hungry bugs, so they make their own chemicals. Many of our medicines come from these chemicals! A plant keeps them in special places, like rooms in a house.

- **Trichomes** are tiny hairs on leaves. Some are like little bottles full of smelly oil. Rub a mint leaf and you pop them!
- **Latex** is a milky juice that flows through tiny pipes inside the plant. When a bug bites, the sticky juice gums up its mouth.
- **Bark** is a tree's coat. The bark of the cinchona tree gave us quinine, a medicine for malaria.
- **Roots** hide underground and store chemicals too.

Drug hunters need to know which part to pick. The medicine is usually hiding in just one part of the plant.
levels.hs:
Plants make thousands of defensive chemicals, but they don't spread them evenly. They package them in special structures, partly so the plant doesn't poison its own cells. Knowing these structures tells a drug hunter which part to collect.

- **Trichomes** are hair-like outgrowths of the plant's outer skin (the **epidermis**). **Glandular trichomes** are tiny chemical factories. In peppermint, they make and store the oil rich in **menthol**.
- **Latex** is a milky fluid made in cells called **laticifers**. When a leaf or stem is cut, latex oozes out, gluing insect mouthparts and delivering toxins. The opium poppy stores its alkaloids in latex, and papaya latex contains **papain**, an enzyme that breaks down proteins.
- **Bark**, to a pharmacognosist, means the tissues outside the **vascular cambium** (the growth layer that makes wood): the corky outer layer plus the living inner bark.
- **Roots and rhizomes** store compounds underground. A **rhizome**, like ginger, is really an underground stem: it has nodes and buds.

**Real example:** Andean **cinchona** trees concentrate **quinine** in their bark. For centuries, bark was stripped and powdered to treat malaria, and in 1820 the French chemists Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine from it. Willow bark similarly contains **salicin**, a natural forerunner of aspirin.
levels.college:
Specialized metabolites are often toxic to the plant that makes them. Plants solve this storage problem with anatomy: they make or accumulate compounds in dedicated cells, cavities and tissues. This compartmentation explains why the crude 'drug' is usually one organ, not the whole plant.

**Secretory structures in leaves and stems**
- **Glandular trichomes**: epidermal hairs whose secretory head cells make terpenes and other compounds. In peppermint (Mentha × piperita), **peltate** trichomes have a disc of secretory cells that push oil into a space under the lifted cuticle; menthol is made there. In Artemisia annua, glandular trichomes produce the antimalarial **artemisinin**.
- **Secretory cavities and ducts**: citrus peel oil glands, resin canals in pines.
- **Idioblasts**: scattered single cells, unlike their neighbors, that store alkaloids, crystals or oils.

**Laticifers**
- **Articulated** laticifers form from chains of cells whose end walls dissolve, as in opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) and the rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis).
- **Non-articulated** laticifers are single, enormous, branching cells that grow with the plant, as in many Euphorbia species.
- Latex is under pressure, so wounding releases it instantly. It can carry alkaloids, proteases such as papain, or irritant diterpene esters.

**Bark**
Pharmacognostic bark comprises the **periderm** (cork, cork cambium, phelloderm) plus the **secondary phloem**. Examples: Cinchona (quinine), Salix (salicin), cinnamon (inner bark), and Pacific yew (Taxus brevifolia), the original source of the cancer drug **paclitaxel**.

**Roots and rhizomes**
Roots are not just storage organs; some are the main factories. Tobacco makes **nicotine** in its roots and sends it to the leaves through the xylem; belladonna makes tropane alkaloids in its roots. True roots lack nodes, while **rhizomes** (ginger, Podophyllum) are stems, a difference that matters when describing and authenticating material. Medicinal roots include Rauvolfia serpentina (reserpine) and licorice (glycyrrhizin).
levels.phd:
The organizing principle is spatial separation of biosynthesis, storage and deployment. This limits autotoxicity and places defenses where attack happens.

**Trichomes as isolated factories.** Peppermint peltate trichomes carry eight secretory cells on a short stalk, with oil collecting in a subcuticular cavity. Because these heads can be mechanically detached, Croteau, Gershenzon and colleagues isolated nearly pure secretory-cell preparations and mapped the menthol pathway, showing that the monoterpene machinery is essentially confined to these cells. In A. annua, artemisinin is made in 10-celled biseriate glandular trichomes; amorpha-4,11-diene synthase and the cytochrome P450 **CYP71AV1** are expressed in the apical secretory cells, so artemisinin content tracks trichome density.

**Laticifers and multicellular pathways.** Latex occurs in roughly 10% of flowering plant species across more than 40 families, and laticifers evolved independently many times. In opium poppy, the benzylisoquinoline pathway spans three phloem cell types: transcripts concentrate in companion cells, most biosynthetic enzymes sit in **sieve elements**, and alkaloids accumulate in adjacent articulated laticifers (Bird, Franceschi and Facchini, 2003). Intermediates or products must therefore move between cells. Agrawal and Konno argued that latex functions chiefly in defense, supported by specialist insects that cut leaf veins to drain latex before feeding.

**Root-to-shoot synthesis.** Dawson's 1940s grafting experiments showed that tobacco scions on tomato rootstocks contained little nicotine, whereas tomato scions on tobacco roots accumulated it: nicotine is made in roots and moved upward in the xylem. Similarly, hyoscyamine 6β-hydroxylase, which forms scopolamine, is expressed in root pericycle cells of tropane-producing Solanaceae (Hashimoto and colleagues, 1991).

**Bark chemistry.** Bark compounds accumulate in phloem parenchyma, ray cells and cork, and concentrations vary across layers and with tree age. Paclitaxel in Pacific yew bark is present at only around 0.01% of dry weight, which is why supply became a crisis once the drug proved effective.

**Nuance.** The site of accumulation is not necessarily the site of synthesis. Sampling only the storage organ can mislead pathway discovery, as the poppy and tobacco cases show.
levels.expert:
**Imaging where chemistry lives.** Mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI, DESI) now maps alkaloids and terpenes at near-cellular resolution in tissue sections, and laser-capture microdissection enables cell-type transcriptomics. Single-cell RNA-seq of Catharanthus roseus leaves (2022–2023) confirmed that the vinblastine precursor pathway is split across cell types: early iridoid steps in internal phloem-associated parenchyma, middle steps in the epidermis, and late vindoline steps in rare idioblasts and laticifers. Bulk extracts of ground leaves average these signals and can hide candidate genes expressed in a few cells.

**Engineering the compartment.** Trichome-specific promoters (for example, the CYP71AV1 promoter) let researchers overexpress pathway genes or transcription factors only in glandular trichomes, avoiding whole-plant growth penalties. A. annua lines bred or engineered for denser trichomes give more artemisinin. Because roots are often the factory, **hairy root cultures**, induced by Rhizobium rhizogenes (formerly Agrobacterium rhizogenes), offer genetically stable, hormone-independent production of root metabolites such as tropane alkaloids.

**Sustainability and supply.** Bark and root harvests are often lethal or slow to recover. Paclitaxel from Pacific yew bark meant killing trees; supply shifted to semisynthesis from 10-deacetylbaccatin III extracted from renewable needles of European yew (Taxus baccata), and later to plant cell fermentation. Prunus africana bark, harvested for prostate remedies, was listed on CITES Appendix II in 1995 after overexploitation; wild American ginseng root is also CITES-listed.

**Clinical and safety notes.** Euphorbia latex contains phorbol and ingenol esters that are potent irritants. Ingenol mebutate from E. peplus was approved for actinic keratosis, then withdrawn in the EU in 2020 over skin-cancer concerns. Hevea latex proteins cause type I latex allergy, a known occupational hazard for clinicians. Collectors sampling latex-bearing plants use gloves and eye protection.

**Pitfalls and open questions.** Substituting a rhizome for a root, inner for whole bark, or the wrong tissue layer changes composition and can invalidate a study. The transporters linking compartments are only partly mapped: tobacco MATE-type transporters load nicotine into vacuoles, but how intermediates cross from poppy sieve elements into laticifers is still unresolved.

keyPoints: Plants store defensive chemicals in special structures, partly to avoid poisoning themselves
Glandular trichomes are hair-like chemical factories (menthol in mint, artemisinin in Artemisia)
Latex is made in laticifers: articulated (poppy, rubber) or non-articulated (Euphorbia)
Pharmacognostic bark is all tissue outside the vascular cambium (quinine, salicin, paclitaxel)
Rhizomes are underground stems with nodes; roots can be the factory, as for nicotine
Where a compound accumulates is not always where it is made

test.q: What are trichomes?
choices: Tubes that carry water up the stems
Pores that open for gas exchange
Hair-like growths on the epidermis
Cells that divide to produce new bark
test.explain: Trichomes are epidermal hairs; glandular ones make and store chemicals. Pores for gas exchange are stomata, and water-carrying tubes are xylem.

test.q: Peppermint's glandular trichomes are the main site of production of:
choices: Menthol
Salicin
Morphine
Quinine
test.explain: Peppermint's peltate glandular trichomes make the oil rich in menthol. Quinine and salicin come from bark, and morphine from poppy latex.

test.q: Latex is produced and stored in specialized cells called:
choices: Laticifers
Stomata
Sieve plates
Tracheids
test.explain: Laticifers are the cells or cell chains that hold latex. Tracheids conduct water, and stomata are leaf pores.

test.q: The latex-producing cells of the opium poppy are classed as:
choices: Resin canals lined by secretory cells
Non-articulated: one giant branching cell
Glandular hairs on the capsule surface
Articulated: chains of fused cells
test.explain: Poppy laticifers are articulated, formed from cell chains whose end walls dissolve. Single giant branching laticifers occur in many Euphorbia species.

test.q: In pharmacognosy, the term 'bark' refers to:
choices: The wood inside the vascular cambium
The waxy cuticle covering young stems
The dead outer cork layer by itself
Tissues outside the vascular cambium
test.explain: Pharmacognostic bark includes the periderm plus the secondary phloem, everything outside the cambium. Cork alone is just the outermost part.

test.q: Which cancer drug was first obtained from the bark of the Pacific yew?
choices: Quinine
Glycyrrhizin
Paclitaxel
Reserpine
test.explain: Paclitaxel was first isolated from Taxus brevifolia bark. Quinine comes from Cinchona bark, reserpine from Rauvolfia root, and glycyrrhizin from licorice root.

test.q: Ginger's underground part is a rhizome rather than a true root because it:
choices: Has nodes and buds like a stem
Stores no starch or essential oil
Contains a network of latex tubes
Develops from the seed's first leaf
test.explain: Rhizomes are underground stems, so they have nodes and buds. True roots lack nodes.

test.q: Where is nicotine mainly made in the tobacco plant?
choices: In the stem bark, close to the phloem
In the roots, then carried to leaves
In flowers, then sent down to roots
In leaf trichomes, where it is stored
test.explain: Tobacco synthesizes nicotine in its roots and moves it to the leaves in the xylem, as grafting experiments showed.

test.q: Why do plants often keep toxic compounds in special structures such as trichomes or laticifers?
choices: To shield their own cells from the toxins
To make the toxins easier for pollinators to find
To convert the toxins into sugars overnight
To pump the toxins into the surrounding soil
test.explain: Compartmentation limits self-poisoning (autotoxicity) and places defenses where attackers bite.

test.q: Quinine is extracted from the bark of the ___ tree.
test.explain: Andean Cinchona trees store quinine in their bark; Pelletier and Caventou isolated it in 1820.

test.q: What protein-digesting enzyme is found in papaya latex?
test.explain: Papain is a protease carried in papaya latex, one example of the defensive proteins latex can contain.

test.explain: Salicin from Salix bark is the natural compound behind the development of aspirin.

advancedTest.q: Tobacco shoots grafted onto tomato rootstocks contain little nicotine, while tomato shoots on tobacco roots accumulate it. The best conclusion is:
choices: Tomato roots break down nicotine coming from leaves
Nicotine is made mainly in roots, then moved upward
Grafting damages the leaf cells that make nicotine
Leaves need tomato hormones before making nicotine
advancedTest.explain: Nicotine appears in whichever shoot sits on tobacco roots, so roots are the factory. Root degradation would not explain why tomato shoots gain nicotine.

advancedTest.q: In opium poppy, most morphine-pathway enzymes sit in sieve elements, while the alkaloids accumulate in adjacent laticifers. This implies:
choices: Intermediates or products move between cell types
Laticifers run the full pathway on their own
Morphine is made by the capsule's outer epidermis
Sieve elements are the main long-term alkaloid store
advancedTest.explain: If synthesis and storage are in different cells, compounds must be transported between them. That is why site of accumulation is not site of synthesis.

advancedTest.q: Which breeding target would most directly raise artemisinin yield in Artemisia annua?
choices: Denser glandular trichomes on leaves
Greater laticifer branching in stems

lessons.title: Botanical Names, Taxonomy and Voucher Specimens

levels.kid:
Some plants have more than one name, and one name can belong to more than one plant. That can be dangerous! The word 'hemlock' can mean a deadly weed or a harmless pine-like tree.

Scientists fix this by giving every plant one special name made of two words, like a first and last name in reverse. The first word is the group name, called the **genus**. The second word picks out one kind, the **species**. Deadly nightshade is *Atropa belladonna*. Scientists all over the world use that same name.

When scientists study a plant, they press and dry a piece of it and save it as proof. This saved plant is called a **voucher**. It lives in a plant library called a **herbarium**, so anyone can check it later.
levels.hs:
Medicine starts with knowing exactly which plant you have. Common names are unreliable. 'Hemlock' can mean *Conium maculatum*, a deadly weed whose poison killed Socrates, or *Tsuga*, a harmless conifer. 'Ginseng' can mean *Panax ginseng*, *Panax quinquefolius*, or an unrelated shrub sold as 'Siberian ginseng.'

The fix is **binomial nomenclature**, set up by Carl **Linnaeus** in *Species Plantarum* (1753). Every species gets a two-part Latin name:
- the **genus**, capitalized (*Digitalis*)
- the **specific epithet**, lowercase (*purpurea*)
- written in italics, often followed by the author who named it: *Digitalis purpurea* L., where 'L.' means Linnaeus.

Species are grouped into a hierarchy called **taxonomy**: species, genus, family, order, and upward. Plant family names end in **-aceae**, like Solanaceae (nightshades) or Apiaceae (carrot family).

Names alone are not proof. Scientists also make a **voucher specimen**: a pressed, dried, labeled sample of the actual plant studied, stored in a **herbarium** with an accession number. If another lab cannot repeat a result, experts can re-examine the voucher to confirm what the plant really was.

A real example of why this matters: in Belgium in the early 1990s, a slimming remedy meant to contain *Stephania tetrandra* was made with *Aristolochia fangchi*, because both were sold under the Chinese name 'fang ji.' The swap caused severe kidney failure in many women.
levels.college:
Accurate identification is the foundation of pharmacognosy: a chemical or pharmacological result is only as good as the identity of the starting material.

**The rules of naming.** Plant, algal and fungal names are governed by the **International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)**, revised at each International Botanical Congress (Shenzhen Code 2018, Madrid Code 2024). Key principles:
- **Priority**: the earliest validly published name wins, counted from 1 May 1753 for most plants.
- **Types**: every name is permanently attached to a type, usually a specimen.
- Since 2012, new names may be described in English or Latin and published electronically.
- Cultivated varieties ('cultivars', written in single quotes) follow a separate code, the ICNCP. Hybrids carry a multiplication sign, as in *Mentha* × *piperita* (peppermint).

**Author citations and synonyms.** When a species is moved to a new genus, the original author goes in parentheses. Madagascar periwinkle, source of vinblastine, was described by Linnaeus as *Vinca rosea* L.; it is now *Catharanthus roseus* (L.) G.Don. The original name is the **basionym**, and old names become **synonyms**. Literature searches must include synonyms or they miss older data.

**Families.** Names end in **-aceae**, but eight conserved alternatives remain legal: Compositae (Asteraceae), Umbelliferae (Apiaceae), Labiatae (Lamiaceae), Leguminosae (Fabaceae), Cruciferae (Brassicaceae), Gramineae (Poaceae), Palmae (Arecaceae), Guttiferae (Clusiaceae). Flowering-plant families now follow the DNA-based **Angiosperm Phylogeny Group** system (APG IV, 2016).

**Voucher specimens.** A voucher is a pressed, dried, mounted sample, ideally with flowers or fruit, labeled with collector, collection number, date, GPS location, habitat, and the identifier (determiner). It is deposited in a herbarium listed in *Index Herbariorum* (for example K for Kew, MO for Missouri) and cited by accession number in publications. Many journals now require voucher citation for plant-based studies.
levels.phd:
Nomenclature and taxonomy are distinct. The ICN regulates which name is correct for a given circumscription, but not the circumscription itself: whether *Cimicifuga* is a separate genus or part of *Actaea* is a scientific judgment. When Compton and colleagues (1998) used morphological and molecular data to sink *Cimicifuga* into *Actaea*, black cohosh became *Actaea racemosa* L. The name changed, the plant did not, and pharmacological databases indexed under one name silently lost records filed under the other.

**Types versus vouchers.** A **holotype** is the single specimen designated by the author as the name-bearer; duplicates are **isotypes**; a **lectotype** is chosen later when no holotype was designated, a **neotype** replaces lost material, and an **epitype** clarifies an ambiguous type. A voucher, by contrast, anchors a *study* to a specimen. Type fixes what a name means; voucher fixes what a researcher actually used.

**Fungi.** The Melbourne Code (effective 2013) ended dual nomenclature, in which one fungus could carry separate names for its sexual (teleomorph) and asexual (anamorph) states: one fungus, one name. New fungal names must also be registered in a recognized repository such as MycoBank.

**Phylogeny predicts chemistry.** Because biosynthetic pathways are inherited, relatives tend to share compound classes: tropane alkaloids across Solanaceae, benzylisoquinoline alkaloids in Papaveraceae and related families. Saslis-Lagoudakis and colleagues (2012, *PNAS*) showed that medicinal plants from unrelated traditional systems cluster in the same lineages, suggesting phylogeny can guide bioprospecting. Accurate placement is therefore predictive, not merely clerical.

**The cost of failure.** The Belgian 'Chinese herb nephropathy' outbreak (Vanherweghem et al., *Lancet*, 1993) arose from vernacular ambiguity: Han fang ji (*Stephania tetrandra*) and Guang fang ji (*Aristolochia fangchi*). Aristolochic acids form DNA adducts; over 100 patients developed progressive renal fibrosis, many needing dialysis or transplant, and a high rate of urothelial carcinoma followed. The condition is now called **aristolochic acid nephropathy**. Pharmaceutical Latin names (for example *Digitalis purpureae folium*, the leaf) add another naming layer that must be mapped to accepted species names.
levels.expert:
In practice, identity errors arise less from bad botany than from broken chains of documentation between field, supplier, lab and paper.

**Workflow essentials:**
- Collect fertile material (flowers or fruit), make several duplicates, and have identification confirmed by a specialist in the group, ideally one who has monographed it.
- For purchased crude drugs, retain a sample of the actual batch, record supplier and lot, and deposit it as a drug-sample voucher; a herbarium sheet of a different plant proves nothing about the powder you extracted.
- Resolve names against Plants of the World Online or World Flora Online, and map trade and pharmacopoeial names with Kew's **Medicinal Plant Names Services (MPNS)**. Report the full accepted name with author and APG family.
- Follow reporting standards such as the **ConPhyMP** consensus (Heinrich et al., 2022) for characterizing extracts.
- Secure access and benefit-sharing permits under the **Nagoya Protocol** (in force 2014) before collecting abroad; papers and patents can be challenged without them.

**Clinical relevance.** Japanese star anise (*Illicium anisatum*) contains anisatin, a GABA-A receptor antagonist; it closely resembles culinary *Illicium verum*, and contaminated teas caused seizures and vomiting in infants, prompting a 2003 FDA advisory. Black cohosh products have repeatedly been found adulterated with Asian *Actaea* species, confounding case reports of liver injury. In any suspected herb toxicity, the identity of the product consumed is the first unknown.

**Herbaria as data.** Mass digitization (GBIF, iDigBio) turns millions of sheets into searchable occurrence records. Old specimens yield DNA and even metabolite profiles, enabling retrospective checks of historical material, though degradation and past pesticide treatments complicate chemistry.

**Open problems.** Species concepts are unstable in apomictic or hybridizing genera such as *Taraxacum*, *Rubus* and *Mentha*, where 'the species' may be a shifting complex. Name churn from molecular phylogenetics continually fragments the literature, and much older pharmacology cites no voucher at all, leaving some classic findings permanently unverifiable.

Binomial = capitalized genus + lowercase specific epithet, italicized (Linnaeus, 1753)
The ICN governs names via priority and type specimens; family names end in -aceae
Synonyms and author citations track renamed species, e.g. Vinca rosea to Catharanthus roseus
A voucher specimen in a herbarium documents exactly what plant a study used
Misidentification can kill: Aristolochia swapped for Stephania caused kidney failure

lessons.title: Chemotypes, Harvest Timing and Drying: What Changes Potency

levels.kid:
Did you know two thyme plants can look exactly the same but smell different? Inside, each one makes its own mix of chemicals. Scientists call these hidden types **chemotypes**. They are like twins who look alike but love different foods.

The time you pick a plant matters too. Some leaves are strongest just before the flowers open. Roots are often best in autumn, when the plant has packed them full of stored food.

Then the plant must be dried, a bit like grapes turning into raisins. Drying stops mould and keeps the medicine safe. But too much heat can cook away the good-smelling oils.

So the right plant, picked at the right time and dried the right way, makes a stronger, safer medicine.
levels.hs:
In pharmacognosy, the **potency** of a crude drug usually means how much of its active compounds it contains. Two bags of the "same" herb can differ several-fold, for three big reasons.

**1. Chemotypes.** A **chemotype** (or chemovar) is a group of plants of one species that look alike but make a different main chemical. Garden thyme (Thymus vulgaris) has chemotypes dominated by thymol, carvacrol, linalool, geraniol and others. Tea tree (Melaleuca alternifolia) has terpinen-4-ol, 1,8-cineole and terpinolene types. The international standard for tea tree oil favors the terpinen-4-ol type. Chemotypes are mostly set by genes, so a correct species name is not enough to predict chemistry.

**2. Harvest timing.** Compound levels change with:
- **Plant part**: leaves, flowers, roots and bark differ.
- **Growth stage**: many leaf drugs peak around flowering. Peppermint is cut at early flowering, when menthol is high and the unwanted **menthofuran** is still low.
- **Season**: roots are dug in autumn or early spring, when storage reserves are full.
- **Age**: ginseng roots are harvested after 4 to 6 years because ginsenosides build up over time.

**3. Drying.** Fresh plants are mostly water. Drying stops **enzymes** and **microbes** from breaking down the drug. Aromatic herbs are dried gently, because high heat drives off their **volatile oils**.
levels.college:
Variation in a crude drug's chemistry comes from genotype, environment, developmental stage and post-harvest handling. Pharmacopoeias manage this by setting minimum contents of **marker compounds** (for example, total alkaloids in belladonna leaf, or sennosides in senna leaf) rather than trusting the label.

**Chemotypes and their causes.** Chemotypes usually reflect differences in genes for key biosynthetic enzymes, such as terpene synthases that decide which monoterpene skeleton is made. Environment then modulates expression: light, UV, temperature, water and nutrient supply all shift secondary metabolism. Basil (Ocimum basilicum) chemotypes rich in linalool, methyl chavicol (estragole) or methyl eugenol show how one species can yield very different oils.

**Developmental and timing effects.**
- Mint leaf oils mature over weeks: menthone is reduced to menthol as leaves age.
- Artemisia annua stores the antimalarial **artemisinin** in glandular trichomes, with levels traditionally highest just before or around flowering.
- St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) is cut at flowering because hypericin and hyperforin concentrate in flowers and buds.
- Bark is often stripped in spring, when the active cambium lets it peel; cinchona bark alkaloids rise with tree age.

**Post-harvest chemistry.** Cutting a plant does not stop its metabolism. Damaged cells lose compartmentalization, so enzymes meet substrates they were kept apart from; glycosides may be hydrolyzed by plant glycosidases. Rapid drying to low moisture (often around 10 to 12% or below) halts this and blocks mould. Temperature is chosen by compound class: volatile-oil drugs are dried at roughly 30 to 40 °C, sturdier drugs at higher temperatures.

Sometimes post-harvest enzyme action is wanted, called **curing** or fermentation:
- **Vanilla**: beta-glucosidase releases vanillin from glucovanillin.
- **Frangula bark** is stored about a year or heat-treated so harsh-acting **anthrones** oxidize to milder anthraquinone forms.
- **Ginger**: heat and drying dehydrate gingerols into more pungent **shogaols**.
levels.phd:
**Genetics and ecology of chemotypes.** The classic system is Thymus vulgaris around Saint-Martin-de-Londres in southern France, studied by Vernet, Gouyon and later John Thompson. About six chemotypes (geraniol, alpha-terpineol, thujanol, linalool, carvacrol, thymol) are controlled by an epistatic series of loci acting along the monoterpene pathway: the non-phenolic geraniol type is dominant, while the phenolic thymol and carvacrol types behave as recessive. Distribution is not random. Phenolic types dominate warm, dry lowland sites, whereas non-phenolic types dominate cold basins with hard winter frosts, where phenolic plants survive less well. Chemotype frequency thus tracks selection by climate, herbivores and neighbouring plants (via allelopathic effects in soil).

A cleaner single-locus case is Cannabis sativa: de Meijer and colleagues (2003) showed that codominant alleles at one locus encode THCA synthase or CBDA synthase, which compete for the shared precursor cannabigerolic acid; heterozygotes give intermediate ratios. Ploidy can also define chemotypes. In Acorus calamus, diploid North American plants contain essentially no **beta-asarone**, while triploid European and especially tetraploid Asian cytotypes can be dominated by it, a concern because beta-asarone is genotoxic and carcinogenic in rodents.

**Developmental regulation.** In peppermint, monoterpene biosynthesis in glandular trichomes is a tightly timed burst in young leaves. Mahmoud and Croteau (2001) showed that menthofuran synthase, a cytochrome P450, diverts pulegone to menthofuran; antisense suppression lowered both. Later work showed menthofuran down-regulates pulegone reductase, so stressed plants accumulate both off-flavour compounds.

**Post-harvest as part of biosynthesis.** High-artemisinin A. annua chemotypes accumulate dihydroartemisinic acid (linked to strong DBR2 expression), whereas low-artemisinin types accumulate artemisinic acid. Conversion of dihydroartemisinic acid to artemisinin is largely non-enzymatic photo-oxidation via singlet oxygen, so it continues in harvested leaves; field- or sun-drying can raise artemisinin per dry weight.

**Environment.** The growth-differentiation balance hypothesis predicts that moderate stress, which slows growth more than photosynthesis, diverts carbon into secondary metabolites. Concentrations often rise under drought, yet biomass falls, so total yield per hectare can drop.
levels.expert:
**Clinical consequences of chemical variability.** St John's wort shows why chemistry, not species name, predicts effects. Products are often standardized to **hypericin**, yet **hyperforin** is the main activator of the nuclear receptor **PXR**, which induces **CYP3A4** and **P-glycoprotein**. Hyperforin content depends on flowering stage, plant part and storage (it oxidizes readily), so two hypericin-matched products can differ greatly in interaction risk. Studies of low-hyperforin extracts found much weaker enzyme induction. Clinicians therefore cannot assume products are interchangeable. Principle: standardize to the constituent that drives the outcome you care about, whether efficacy or toxicity.

**Toxic chemotypes and regulatory limits.** The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee has issued public statements limiting exposure to beta-asarone (Acorus), estragole (basil, fennel) and thujone (wormwood, sage), because chemotype choice can change exposure many-fold. Sourcing a low-risk chemotype is usually easier than removing a compound later.

**Quality systems.** The WHO guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP, 2003) and the EMA GACP guideline require documentation of seed origin, site, harvest stage, time of collection and drying conditions. Wild collection mixes chemotypes uncontrollably; cultivating clonal or seed-stable elite lines narrows variation. Molecular breeding produced high-artemisinin A. annua lines after Graham and colleagues (Science, 2010) mapped loci affecting artemisinin yield.

**Analytical pitfalls.**
- Results per fresh weight, per dry weight or per hectare are not interchangeable.
- A single marker may miss synergists or co-occurring toxins; untargeted metabolomics (LC-MS, NMR) with chemometrics (PCA, PLS-DA) captures chemotype fingerprints better.
- Drying and grinding create artefacts (shogaols in ginger, baldrinals from unstable valerian valepotriates), so the analysed profile may not match the living plant.
- Stored herbs lose volatiles and oxidize; stability testing must track the relevant markers.

**Open questions.** How stable are chemotypes under climate change, as heat, CO2 and drought shift both selection and gene expression? How much variation comes from epigenetics, or from endophytic microbes that can modify metabolite profiles? And can field sensors such as near-infrared spectroscopy pinpoint the day of peak content for harvest?

Heat switches on a synthase gene silent in living leaves
Leaf-surface microbes secrete artemisinin as they grow
advancedTest.explain: Dihydroartemisinic acid converts to artemisinin by largely non-enzymatic photo-oxidation, which continues in harvested leaves. Water loss cannot explain a rise expressed per dry weight.

advancedTest.q: Drought raises a root drug's alkaloid concentration by 30% (dry-weight basis) but cuts root biomass by 40%. Compared with an unstressed crop, alkaloid harvested per hectare is:
choices: About the same
About 22% lower
About 30% higher
About 10% lower
advancedTest.explain: Total yield equals concentration times biomass: 1.3 x 0.6 = 0.78, about 22% lower. Higher concentration does not guarantee more product per hectare.

advancedTest.q: A patient stable on a CYP3A4 substrate switches from a low-hyperforin St John's wort extract to a high-hyperforin one. The most likely result is:
choices: Higher drug levels from CYP3A4 inhibition by hypericin
No change, since both share one standardized marker
Lower drug levels from PXR-driven CYP3A4 induction
Higher drug levels from reduced P-glycoprotein expression
advancedTest.explain: Hyperforin activates PXR, inducing CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and lowering substrate levels. Hypericin-matched standardization does not capture hyperforin differences.

lessons.title: Authenticating Crude Drugs: Microscopy and DNA Barcoding

levels.kid:
When you buy apples, you can tell them from oranges just by looking. Plant medicines are often sold as dry, crumbly powder, though, and a pile of brown powder all looks the same! So scientists act like detectives to check that it is the right plant.

First they use a **microscope**. Hidden in the powder are tiny clues: little hairs, sparkly crystals and round starch grains. Each plant has its own pattern, like a fingerprint.

Next they read the plant's **DNA**, the secret instruction code inside every cell. A short piece of it works like the barcode on a cereal box in a shop. It tells you the plant's name.

Why bother? Some plants have look-alike cousins that are poisonous. Checking keeps people safe.
levels.hs:
A **crude drug** is plant (or animal or fungal) material that has only been dried or cut, such as a dried root, leaf or bark sold as powder or tea. **Authentication** means proving that a sample really is the species and plant part on the label.

This matters because once a plant is chopped and dried, its shape is gone, and swaps are easy. Swaps can be accidental (two plants share a common name) or deliberate (a cheaper plant is substituted).

Scientists use several layers of evidence:
- **Macroscopic and sensory checks**: shape, color, smell, taste and fracture of the whole drug.
- **Microscopy**: cells and tiny structures that survive drying, such as leaf pores, hairs and crystals.
- **Chemical fingerprinting**: separating the plant's chemicals, for example by thin-layer chromatography, to see a characteristic pattern.
- **DNA barcoding**: reading a short, standard stretch of DNA and matching it to a reference database.

A real example: in the early 1990s, a Belgian slimming clinic gave patients a powder meant to contain *Stephania tetrandra*. Both it and *Aristolochia fangchi* shared the Chinese name fang ji, and the batch actually contained Aristolochia. Its **aristolochic acid** caused kidney failure in many patients, and some later developed urinary tract cancers. Careful authentication would have caught the swap.
levels.college:
Pharmacopoeias (European, British, Chinese and others) describe each herbal drug with identification tests. Microscopy of the powdered drug is the classic workhorse because many cell features survive drying and grinding.

**Diagnostic microscopic features:**
- **Stomata**: the pattern of guard cells and surrounding subsidiary cells is classified as anomocytic, anisocytic, diacytic or paracytic. Senna leaflets, for example, have paracytic stomata.
- **Trichomes**: plant hairs, unicellular or multicellular, glandular or covering, often with distinctive warts or heads.
- **Calcium oxalate crystals**: needle bundles called **raphides** (as in squill), single prisms, or star-like clusters called **druses** (large druses are typical of rhubarb).
- **Starch grains**: size, shape and the position of the hilum. Under polarized light they show a dark Maltese cross.
- **Lignified tissue**: fibers, vessels and stone cells (sclereids).

**Stains** reveal chemistry in cells: phloroglucinol with hydrochloric acid turns lignin red, iodine turns starch blue-black, and Sudan III colors oils and fats.

**Quantitative leaf constants** help separate close species: the **stomatal index** (stomata as a percentage of all epidermal cells, S/(S+E) x 100) and the vein-islet number per square millimeter.

**DNA barcoding** works in four steps: extract DNA, amplify a standard region by PCR, sequence it, and compare it with a reference library such as BOLD or GenBank. Animals use the mitochondrial gene COI, but plant mitochondrial DNA evolves too slowly to separate species. Plants therefore use the chloroplast genes **rbcL** and **matK** as the core barcode, often supplemented by the nuclear **ITS2** spacer or the chloroplast psbA-trnH spacer.

Each method has limits. Microscopy needs expert eyes and fails on extracts; DNA identifies species but says nothing about how potent the material is. That is why identity tests are paired with chemical assays.
levels.phd:
DNA barcoding began with Hebert and colleagues' 2003 proposal of COI for animals. For land plants, low mitochondrial substitution rates and frequent genome rearrangement ruled COI out. After competing proposals, the CBOL Plant Working Group (2009, PNAS) adopted **rbcL + matK** as the core plant barcode: rbcL amplifies easily but varies little, matK varies more but has troublesome primers. Together they discriminated roughly 72% of species tested. Chen and colleagues (2010) argued that the nuclear **ITS2** region identified about 92.7% of the medicinal plant species they sampled, and ITS2 (with psbA-trnH as a supplement) became central to Chinese materia medica barcoding.

Technical pitfalls are substantial:
- **DNA degradation**: heating, boiling and long storage fragment DNA, so full-length barcodes fail. **Mini-barcodes** of roughly 100 to 250 base pairs improve recovery.
- **PCR inhibitors**: polysaccharides and polyphenols co-purify and block amplification, demanding modified extraction protocols.
- **Reference library quality**: a match is only as good as the reference. Misidentified GenBank entries propagate errors, so references should trace to vouchered specimens.
- **Biological limits**: recent radiation, hybridization and incomplete lineage sorting leave closely related species (for example within *Panax* or *Actaea*) with nearly identical barcodes; ITS also has multiple paralogous copies.

Newmaster and colleagues (2013, BMC Medicine) barcoded commercial herbal products and reported widespread substitution and unlabeled fillers such as rice, soybean and wheat. In 2015 the New York Attorney General used barcoding to challenge store-brand supplements, but critics noted that many were standardized **extracts**, where solvent extraction and purification remove most DNA. A negative result in an extract is inconclusive, and detected filler DNA might come from excipients.

**DNA metabarcoding** (high-throughput sequencing of amplicons) detects multiple species in mixtures, which suits multi-herb formulas. However, read counts are distorted by amplification bias, copy-number differences and DNA quality, so metabarcoding is semi-quantitative at best. Trace reads may reflect pollen, dust or lab contamination rather than a meaningful ingredient. Barcoding answers "what species?", not "how much?" or "which part?"
levels.expert:
Authentication failures produce recognizable clinical patterns, and the clinician-scientist should know them.

- **Aristolochic acid** forms DNA adducts that leave a mutational signature dominated by A:T to T:A transversions (COSMIC SBS22). Ng and colleagues (2017) found this signature in many hepatocellular carcinomas across Asia, implying exposure far beyond the Belgian cluster. Species-specific qPCR and LC-MS for aristolochic acids now screen formulas for Aristolochia admixture.
- **Japanese star anise** (*Illicium anisatum*) contains **anisatin**, a noncompetitive GABA-A receptor antagonist. Contamination of *Illicium verum* in infant teas has caused seizures and vomiting, prompting a 2003 FDA advisory. The fruits look alike; GC or HPLC fingerprints and DNA separate them.
- In 1997, a plantain product was contaminated with *Digitalis lanata*, causing cardiac glycoside toxicity; foxglove mistaken for comfrey has done the same.

Practical points: when a patient has unexplained toxicity after an herbal product, keep the remaining product and packaging. Identification is a forensic chain, and analyses later need the actual batch.

Regulatory uptake is growing. The British Pharmacopoeia added DNA-based identification in 2017, with holy basil (*Ocimum tenuiflorum*) as the first monograph using it, and the Chinese Pharmacopoeia includes ITS2-based guidelines. Barcoding is positioned as one identity test alongside microscopy and chromatography.

Recent advances:
- **Genome skimming** and whole-plastome "super-barcodes" boost resolution among close relatives.
- Portable **nanopore** sequencing allows identification near harvest sites and borders.
- Rapid targeted assays such as **Bar-HRM** (barcode plus high-resolution melting) and LAMP flag a known adulterant cheaply.
- NMR and LC-MS metabolomics with chemometrics authenticate extracts where DNA is absent.

Open questions: how to set reporting thresholds for trace metabarcoding hits; how to quantify species proportions reliably; how to fill reference libraries for poorly sampled tropical flora; and how to link genetic identity with chemical quality, since a correctly identified plant can still be low in its active constituents.

keyPoints: Authentication proves a crude drug is the correct species and plant part
Microscopy uses stomata, trichomes, crystals, starch grains and lignified cells
Stains help: phloroglucinol-HCl colors lignin red, iodine colors starch blue-black
Core plant DNA barcode is rbcL + matK, often with nuclear ITS2
DNA identifies species but not potency, and often fails on extracts
Swaps like Aristolochia for Stephania caused kidney failure and cancer

test.q: What is the main goal of authenticating a crude drug?
choices: Measuring how much active compound it holds
Confirming it is the correct plant and part
Checking it was grown without pesticides
Testing whether it cures the target disease
test.explain: Authentication is about identity: right species and right plant part. Measuring active compounds is a separate quality assay.

test.q: When iodine is added to powdered plant material, starch grains turn:
choices: Pale green
Yellow-orange
Blue-black
Bright red
test.explain: Iodine stains starch blue-black. Red staining is what phloroglucinol-HCl does to lignin.

test.q: Which stain turns lignified fibers and stone cells red?
choices: Sudan III in ethanol
Iodine in potassium iodide
Methylene blue in water
Phloroglucinol with HCl
test.explain: Phloroglucinol with hydrochloric acid reacts with lignin to give a red color. Sudan III in ethanol stains oils and fats, iodine in potassium iodide stains starch blue-black, and methylene blue is a general stain for nuclei and cells.

test.q: Which two chloroplast genes form the core plant DNA barcode?
choices: rbcL and matK
ITS1 and actin
16S and 18S rRNA
COI and cytochrome b
test.explain: The CBOL Plant Working Group chose rbcL plus matK. COI is the animal barcode.

test.q: Why is the animal barcode gene COI not used to identify plant species?
choices: COI is too long to sequence in plants
Plants lack mitochondria in their cells
Plant COI is destroyed by drying
Plant mitochondria evolve too slowly
test.explain: Plant mitochondrial DNA changes too slowly to tell species apart. Plants do have mitochondria, so that distractor is false.

test.q: In the 1990s Belgian slimming-clinic case, swapping Stephania for Aristolochia caused:
choices: Seizures and brain swelling
Heart rhythm disturbances
Severe liver inflammation
Kidney failure and cancers
test.explain: Aristolochic acid caused kidney failure, and some patients later developed urinary tract cancers.

test.q: Why might DNA barcoding fail to identify a standardized herbal extract?
choices: Extracts are made from animal tissue
Chloroplast genes vanish after harvest
Extraction degrades or removes the DNA
Extracts contain too many plant species
test.explain: Solvent extraction and purification strip out most DNA, so a negative result in an extract is inconclusive.

test.q: Large star-shaped clusters of calcium oxalate, typical of rhubarb, are called:
choices: Trichomes
Raphides
Druses
Prisms
test.explain: Druses are cluster crystals. Raphides are needle bundles, and trichomes are plant hairs, not crystals.

test.q: Which question can DNA barcoding NOT answer by itself?
choices: Whether a known toxic look-alike is there
How potent the material is
Whether a filler plant is present
Which species is present
test.explain: DNA tells you which species are present, not how much active compound the material contains. Potency needs chemical assays.

test.q: The ___ index is the percentage of epidermal cells on a leaf that are stomata.
test.explain: Stomatal index = S/(S+E) x 100, a quantitative constant that helps separate close species.

test.q: Which nuclear spacer region did Chen and colleagues (2010) propose for identifying medicinal plants?
test.explain: ITS2 identified about 92.7% of medicinal plant species in their study and is central to Chinese pharmacopoeial barcoding.

test.q: Name the GABA-A antagonist neurotoxin found in Japanese star anise.
test.explain: Anisatin causes seizures; contamination of true star anise teas with Illicium anisatum has poisoned infants.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists check plant medicine powders?
choices: To change the plant's color
To make the plant grow bigger
To be sure it is the right plant
kidTest.explain: Powders look alike, so scientists check that the plant is the right one.

kidTest.q: What tiny clues can a microscope show in plant powder?
choices: Leaves and roots
Hairs and crystals
Seeds and flowers
kidTest.explain: Tiny hairs, crystals and starch grains act like a plant's fingerprint.

kidTest.q: Reading a plant's DNA name tag is a lot like:
choices: A clock telling a plant's age
A shop code naming a product
A map showing where plants grow
kidTest.explain: A short piece of DNA works like a barcode in a shop: it tells you the plant's name.

kidTest.q: What could happen if a poisonous look-alike plant is used?
choices: The medicine works twice as fast
The person could get sick
The medicine lasts much longer
kidTest.explain: Some look-alike plants are poisonous, so mix-ups can make people sick.

kidTest.q: Scientists look at plant powder with a m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A microscope makes tiny clues big enough to see.

advancedTest.q: In the 2015 New York supplement investigation, many products showed no DNA of the labeled herb. What is the most defensible interpretation?
choices: Chloroplast DNA is unstable at room temperature
The rbcL primers were designed for animal tissue
The labeled herb was absent, proving deliberate fraud
Processing removes DNA, so negatives are inconclusive
advancedTest.explain: Many products were extracts, where DNA is largely removed. Absence of DNA is not proof of absence of the herb; chemical methods are needed.

advancedTest.q: Metabarcoding of a ginkgo product detects a few reads from a weed species. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The ginkgo label is false and the product is fake
Trace reads may be incidental and need follow-up
The weed is the main ingredient of the product
The method mistook ginkgo reads for weed reads
advancedTest.explain: Read counts are not quantitative and traces can come from pollen, dust or contamination. Confirmation with targeted and chemical methods is needed.

advancedTest.q: rbcL + matK fail to separate two closely related Panax species. The most likely reason is:
choices: Roots lack plastid DNA for amplification
Recent divergence leaves few sequence differences
Chloroplast genes mutate too fast to compare
Ginsenosides degrade the PCR primers directly
advancedTest.explain: Recent radiation, hybridization and incomplete lineage sorting leave near-identical barcodes. Higher-resolution markers or genome skimming help.

advancedTest.q: DNA confirms Illicium verum in a tea linked to infant seizures. Why still run a GC or HPLC fingerprint?
choices: It detects bacterial growth in the dried fruit
It proves the plant's geographic origin precisely
It replaces microscopy as the pharmacopoeial test
It reveals toxin levels and admixture DNA may miss
advancedTest.explain: DNA shows that a species is present, not toxin content or the proportion of a minor Illicium anisatum admixture. Chemistry can measure anisatin-related markers.
